glossary.definition: An event that could have caused harm but did not.
A rating set from the level of harm, actual or potential, defined by the organization.
An action taken to remove the cause of an incident so it does not recur.
The role accountable for decisions and records in a defined workflow.
An event that caused harm, damage, or a stoppage.
A condition someone noticed before any event occurred.
Statements that a software demonstration can prove or fail to prove, derived from the plant's own problem statement, process map, and decision table.
A step in the reporting process after which no record shows a decision was made, leaving a report unresolved.
A record showing which roles may file, read, rate, investigate, or close a report, used to evaluate whether access can be limited by role and reviewed.
A structured document recording vendor answers on setup effort, cost, and support responsibilities, used as the evaluation record for the final subsection.
A record of chosen QR code or access-point locations on the floor, including the person responsible for each and the check schedule.
The record created when a reviewer first reads a new report, showing who reviewed it, when, and what decision was made.
Fields completed by the floor reporter at the point of work, covering description, who was affected, location, time, injury or damage indicator, and optional photo.
Fields completed by the first reviewer when reading a new report, covering category and hand-off to the severity process.
Fields completed later in the process covering causes, evidence, and conclusions.
The record of the final form design stating field name, who completes it, whether it is required, and what values it accepts.
The record created when an investigator is assigned to an investigation, naming the investigator, the scope and the date, and showing every subsequent change with a date and a name.
The record kept with the incident of all items collected during an investigation, noting what each item is, who collected it, when and where it is held.

The record of what the investigator and supervisor concluded caused or contributed to the event, distinguishing observed facts, reported information and inferences, and showing which evidence supports each point.
The accepted output of a completed investigation, comprising the cause statement and recommendations, bearing the reviewer's name and the date of acceptance.
The record of what each role or group may see in the dashboard, decided by the safety lead and used to control visibility into incident data.
The record of a committee meeting showing which reports and actions were examined, which patterns were raised, and who will follow up.
A feedback entry or note in the team meeting record showing what was shared with reporters about closed reports, within the plant's privacy rules.
The record of items identified during an audit rehearsal or audit view review, each with an owner and a date for resolution.
A record listing each ISO 45001 clause in scope, the requirement it makes, the records the plant holds as evidence, where they are kept, and who owns them.
The record of the scope of a historical data migration, the mapping of old fields to new ones, decisions about unmapped fields, and the location of the original archive.

The record of the date and method by which the new system becomes the authoritative record for incident and near-miss reports, including parallel-period rules, training schedule, and rollback criteria.
A running record of each time the reporting process failed in a way that mattered, reviewed for repeats and used to prompt process or settings changes.
The record produced by a periodic workflow review, capturing what was sampled, what was found, and what will change.

reviewedChapters.title: Run investigations from a structured record
reviewedChapters.summary: All checks pass. The page matches the plan exactly across four subsections: Assign and scope the investigation, Collect evidence, Analyze causes without blame, and Record conclusions and review. Each subsection contains the required workflow elements (role, input, decision, record, exception) and an evaluation criterion drawn from the plan. The illustrative example in the first subsection is correctly labeled as invented and not a customer result. All ICC Safety capability claims are consistently framed as published descriptions requiring demonstration confirmation, in line with the research source constraints. The ICC page's statement that investigations start from a blank page is correctly presented as a vendor-described pain point rather than measured data. The AI-output review claim appears twice—once in the cause analysis section and once in the conclusions section—but the two occurrences serve distinct purposes (introducing the AI concern in context of cause analysis, and reinforcing it as a reviewer obligation in the conclusions step), so this does not constitute problematic repetition. The Ontario JHSC guide is cited only in the final subsection and with an explicit caution that plants outside Ontario must check their own rules. Links use only the two supplied source URLs (icc-safety and ontario-jhsc-guide) plus an allowed internal site path. No FAQ section appears anywhere in the page, consistent with the plan assigning none. No scope boundary violations were detected; corrective action tracking is appropriately deferred to the next chapter. Word count of approximately 2028 is within acceptable range of the 2000-word target. No previous findings were raised, so none remain unresolved.
